title: Is It Ever Okay For Students To Leave Their Seat Without Permission? eat-without-permission/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a frequently asked question, Linsin explains how to handle the tension between rigid raise-your-hand rules and reasonable exceptions like getting a tissue or sharpening a pencil. His solution is precision: define narrowly and explicitly which actions are exceptions to the raise-your-hand rule, and model exactly what performing them correctly — and incorrectly — looks like, including the specific route a student should take and what not to do, like wandering or bothering classmates. He also stresses specifying times when even approved exceptions are off-limits, such as during direct instruction. Linsin argues that narrow definitions paired with precise modeling remove any excuse for wandering or arguing, since expectations are on record and non-negotiable. He recommends limiting exceptions to just three or four commonly requested needs, spending about thirty minutes teaching and modeling them, and then holding students strictly accountable for any deviation.
points: Defining precisely and narrowly which actions don't require raising a hand prevents both rigidity and abuse of the privilege.
Explicit modeling of both correct and incorrect ways to perform an exception removes ambiguity and excuses.
Teachers should also specify times when even approved exceptions are off-limits, such as during direct instruction.
Limiting exceptions to three or four commonly needed actions keeps the system manageable and clear.
Holding students accountable for any deviation from narrowly defined exceptions produces a calmer, more focused classroom.
quotes: The solution is to define for your students precisely and narrowly what is and isn’t okay and when it is and isn’t okay to do it.
You would then model what getting a tissue looks like—which would include taking a direct route to and from the tissue box without interrupting others.
Explicit modeling lays it all out, puts it on record, and removes any excuse to be up and out of their seats for any other reason or in any other way.
Finally, it’s important that you detail any time or times you don’t want them to be able to get up, like while you’re giving directions or providing instruction, for example.
Narrow definitions and precise modeling are the keys to successfully allowing reasonable exceptions to your rules.
As long as you hold accountable any student who strays even a nanometer from your narrow exceptions, you’ll have a more focused and peaceful classroom.
